cards.name: Price direction: volatility
cards.prompt: Holding everything else fixed, what happens to the price of a put (European or American) when the underlying's volatility $\sigma$ increases?
cards.answer: It increases (calls rise too, European and American alike)
cards.explanation:
An option holder's loss is capped at the premium, while the gain grows with the size of the move.
A higher $\sigma$ widens the distribution of $S_T$ in both directions: the extra upside adds value, and the extra downside is cut off by the $\max(\cdot,0)$.
Put another way, vanilla payoffs are convex in $S$, so more dispersion raises their expected value. That is why vega is positive for both calls and puts.
distractors: It decreases (puts fall while calls rise)
It is unchanged (only calls are sensitive to volatility)
It depends on whether the put is in or out of the money
cards.hint: The payoff $\max(K-S_T,0)$ can't drop below 0, however far $S_T$ rises.

cards.name: Price direction: interest rate
cards.prompt: All else equal, how does an increase in the risk-free rate $r$ affect the value of a call (European or American)?
cards.answer: It increases (while put values fall)
cards.explanation:
The call holder pays $K$ at expiry. A higher $r$ lowers the present value of that payment, so the call is worth more.
The put holder receives $K$ at expiry, and its present value falls, so the put is worth less. In risk-neutral terms the stock drifts at $r$, so a higher $r$ also shifts $S_T$ up.
Caveat: in real markets rates and stock prices move together (a rate cut often lifts stocks), so the change-one-factor answer can be swamped.
distractors: It decreases, since the payoff is discounted at a higher rate
It is unchanged, since $r$ does not appear in the call payoff
It depends on moneyness: up in the money, down out of the money
cards.hint: Who pays the strike, and who receives it?

cards.name: Price direction: dividends
cards.prompt: All else equal, how do larger expected dividends (paid before expiry) affect the value of a call?
cards.answer: It decreases (while put values rise)
cards.explanation:
The option holder does not receive dividends, but the share price drops by roughly the dividend on the ex-dividend date.
A lower expected $S_T$ hurts calls and helps puts. In put-call parity the stock appears as $S-D$, so a larger $D$ lowers $c-p$.
distractors: It increases, since the stock pays out more
It is unchanged; dividends only matter to shareholders
It increases for American calls and decreases for European ones

cards.name: Price direction: time to maturity
cards.prompt: How does a longer time to maturity affect (a) American calls and puts and (b) European calls and puts?
cards.answer: American: both worth more; European: can go either way
cards.explanation:
A longer-dated American option has every exercise opportunity of the shorter one, plus more, so it cannot be worth less.
A European option can only be exercised at its own expiry, so extra time can hurt:
- A large dividend paid between the two expiries can make the shorter-dated call worth more.
- A deep in-the-money put collects $K$ sooner if it expires earlier, which is worth more when rates are positive.
distractors: Both types are always worth more with longer maturity
American: can go either way; European: both worth more
Both types are always worth less with longer maturity
cards.hint: Consider a big dividend between the two expiry dates.

cards.name: Price direction: stock and strike
cards.prompt: How does a call's value react to (a) a higher stock price $S$ and (b) a higher strike $K$? What about a put?
cards.answer: Call: up with $S$, down with $K$; put: down with $S$, up with $K$
cards.explanation:
The call payoff $\max(S_T-K,0)$ is nondecreasing in $S_T$ and nonincreasing in $K$: a higher strike never pays more and sometimes pays less.
The put payoff $\max(K-S_T,0)$ moves the opposite way in both. This holds for European and American options alike.
distractors: Call: up with $S$, up with $K$; put: the reverse
Call: down with $S$, up with $K$; put: the reverse
Call: up with $S$, down with $K$; put: the same as the call

cards.name: Put-call parity
cards.prompt: State put-call parity for European options (same underlying, strike $K$, maturity $T$) on a stock whose dividends before $T$ have present value $D$.
cards.answer: $c+Ke^{-r\tau}=p+S-D$
cards.explanation:
Left side: a call plus a zero-coupon bond paying $K$ at $T$. Right side: a put plus the stock, minus the dividends that the stockholder collects but the option holder does not.
Both portfolios are worth $\max(S_T,K)$ at expiry, so no-arbitrage forces them to cost the same today. Here $\tau=T-t$.
distractors: $c+S=p+Ke^{-r\tau}-D$
$c+Ke^{-r\tau}=p+S+D$
$c+K=p+Se^{-r\tau}-D$
cards.hint: Which side holds the stock, and who gets the dividends?

cards.name: Put-call parity proof
cards.prompt: Write down put-call parity for European options on a non-dividend-paying stock and prove it.
cards.answer: $c+Ke^{-r\tau}=p+S$; both sides pay $\max(S_T,K)$ at $T$
cards.explanation:
Portfolio A: one call plus a zero-coupon bond with face $K$. At $T$ it is worth $(S_T-K)^++K=\max(S_T,K)$.
Portfolio B: one put plus one share (a protective put). At $T$ it is worth $(K-S_T)^++S_T=\max(S_T,K)$.
Neither portfolio has cash flows before $T$. If their prices differed, you could buy the cheaper one and sell the dearer one for a riskless profit. Hence $c+Ke^{-r\tau}=p+S$.
distractors: $c+S=p+Ke^{-r\tau}$; both sides pay $\max(S_T,K)$ at $T$
$c-p=S-K$; both sides pay $S_T-K$ at $T$
$c+K=p+S$; both sides pay $\max(S_T,K)$ at $T$

cards.name: Call price bounds
cards.prompt: Using put-call parity (dividends with present value $D$), what simple lower and upper bounds hold for a European call price $c$?
cards.answer: $S-D-Ke^{-r\tau}\le c\le S$
cards.explanation:
From parity, $c=p+S-D-Ke^{-r\tau}$, and $p\ge0$ gives the lower bound (together with $c\ge0$).
A call can never be worth more than the share, because its payoff $\max(S_T-K,0)$ never exceeds $S_T$. With dividends, $S-D$ is an even tighter cap.
distractors: $S-K\le c\le Ke^{-r\tau}$
$S-D-Ke^{-r\tau}\le c\le Ke^{-r\tau}$
$Ke^{-r\tau}-S\le c\le S-D$

cards.name: American put-call inequality
cards.prompt: For American options put-call parity is no longer an equality. What inequality bounds $C-P$ (American call minus American put, dividends with present value $D$)?
cards.answer: $S-D-K\le C-P\le S-Ke^{-r\tau}$
cards.explanation:
Early exercise rights break the exact equality, but no-arbitrage still keeps $C-P$ inside a band.
- Upper bound: an American put is worth at least the European put, and dividends can only lower the call, so $C-P$ cannot exceed the no-dividend European value $S-Ke^{-r\tau}$.
- Lower bound: a call plus cash $D+K$ is always worth at least a put plus one share, whenever the put is exercised.
With no dividends the band is $S-K\le C-P\le S-Ke^{-r\tau}$.
distractors: $S-Ke^{-r\tau}\le C-P\le S-D-K$
$S-K\le C-P\le S-D-Ke^{-r\tau}$
$C-P=S-D-Ke^{-r\tau}$ exactly

cards.name: Call equals put
cards.prompt: For a non-dividend stock, when is a European call worth exactly the same as a European put with the same strike and maturity?
cards.answer: When $K=Se^{r\tau}$, the forward price
cards.explanation:
Rewrite parity as $c-p=S-Ke^{-r\tau}$. A long call plus a short put pays $S_T-K$ at expiry, which is a forward contract with delivery price $K$, worth $S-Ke^{-r\tau}$ today.
That value is zero exactly when $K$ equals the forward price $Se^{r\tau}$. For $K<Se^{r\tau}$ the call is worth more; for $K>Se^{r\tau}$ the put is.
distractors: When $K=S$ (at the money spot)
When $K=Se^{-r\tau}$
Never; the call is always worth more
cards.hint: Long call plus short put replicates what contract?

cards.name: American vs. European options (A)
cards.prompt: When, if ever, is it optimal to exercise an American call on a non-dividend-paying stock before maturity?
cards.answer: Never: the call is always worth more than $S-K$ (at least $S-Ke^{-r\tau}$), so selling beats exercising
cards.explanation:
Exercising now gives only the intrinsic value $S-K$.
From parity, $c=(S-K)+(K-Ke^{-r\tau})+p$. On top of intrinsic value, the call carries the interest saved by paying $K$ later and the value of an embedded put, and both are nonnegative. So $c>S-K$.
An American call is worth at least the European one, so it also exceeds intrinsic value: selling it, or holding it, beats exercising it. As a result, American and European calls on non-dividend stocks have the same price.
distractors: Once $S$ exceeds $Ke^{r\tau}$, when the call is deep enough in the money
Whenever it is deep in the money, since its time value is then near 0
At any time: its value equals $S-K$, so exercising early costs nothing

cards.name: Call value decomposition
cards.prompt: Use put-call parity to split a European call on a non-dividend stock into three pieces, and name each piece.
cards.answer: $c=(S-K)+(K-Ke^{-r\tau})+p$: intrinsic, interest on strike, put insurance
cards.explanation:
Start from $c-p=S-Ke^{-r\tau}$, then add and subtract $K$.
- $S-K$: what you would get by exercising now.
- $K-Ke^{-r\tau}\ge0$: the benefit of paying the strike later rather than now.
- $p\ge0$: protection against the stock ending below $K$, which exercising would give up.
The last two terms are nonnegative, so the call is worth at least its intrinsic value.
distractors: $c=(S-K)-(K-Ke^{-r\tau})+p$: intrinsic, minus interest, put insurance
$c=(S-K)+(K-Ke^{-r\tau})-p$: intrinsic, interest on strike, minus put
$c=(S-Ke^{-r\tau})+(K-S)+p$: forward, moneyness, put insurance

cards.name: Early exercise: replication argument
cards.prompt: Instead of exercising an in-the-money American call on a non-dividend stock at time $t$ to receive $S-K$, what strategy gives the same cash today plus a positive payoff at $T$?
cards.answer: Keep the call, short one share, lend $K$ at $r$ until $T$
cards.explanation:
Shorting the share brings in $S$, and lending $K$ uses $K$ of it, leaving $S-K$ today, the same as exercising.
At $T$ you hold the call, owe one share and receive $Ke^{r\tau}$:
- If $S_T\le K$: the call expires worthless and you net $Ke^{r\tau}-S_T>0$.
- If $S_T>K$: exercise and deliver the share, netting $Ke^{r\tau}-K>0$.
You get the same money today and a strictly positive payoff later, so exercising early is dominated.
distractors: Keep the call, buy one share, borrow $K$ at $r$ until $T$
Sell the call and buy a put with strike $K$
Keep the call and sell a put with strike $K$

cards.name: Early exercise: Jensen argument
cards.prompt: Give the convexity (Jensen) argument that an American call on a non-dividend stock should not be exercised early. Which inequality results? Here $C(S)=(S-K)^+$.
cards.answer: $C(S_t)\le e^{-r\tau}C(e^{r\tau}S_t)\le e^{-r\tau}\tilde E[C(S_T)]$
cards.explanation:
$C$ is convex with $C(0)=0$, so for $0<\lambda<1$: $C(\lambda S)\le\lambda C(S)+(1-\lambda)C(0)=\lambda C(S)$.
Take $\lambda=e^{-r\tau}$ and $S=e^{r\tau}S_t$ to get $C(S_t)\le e^{-r\tau}C(e^{r\tau}S_t)$.
Under the risk-neutral measure $\tilde E[S_T]=e^{r\tau}S_t$, so Jensen's inequality gives $C(e^{r\tau}S_t)\le\tilde E[C(S_T)]$.
So the payoff from exercising now, $C(S_t)$, is never more than the discounted value of holding to expiry.
distractors: $C(S_t)\ge e^{-r\tau}C(e^{r\tau}S_t)\ge e^{-r\tau}\tilde E[C(S_T)]$
$C(S_t)\le e^{r\tau}C(e^{-r\tau}S_t)\le e^{r\tau}\tilde E[C(S_T)]$
$C(S_t)=e^{-r\tau}\tilde E[C(S_T)]$ because $C$ is linear

cards.name: American put early exercise
cards.prompt: A put's payoff is also convex in $S$, yet early exercise of an American put on a non-dividend stock can be optimal. Where does the call argument break down?
cards.answer: A put pays $K$ at $S=0$, so $P(\lambda S)\le\lambda P(S)$ fails; in fact $P(\lambda S)\ge\lambda P(S)$
cards.explanation:
The call argument needs $C(0)=0$ to turn convexity into $C(\lambda S)\le\lambda C(S)$. For a put, $P(0)=K>0$, and the inequality flips.
Intuitively, a deep in-the-money put is already close to its maximum payoff $K$. Exercising now lets you start earning interest on $K$, which can outweigh the little optionality left. So American puts can be worth more than European puts even with no dividends.
distractors: The put payoff is concave in $S$, so Jensen's inequality reverses
Puts have negative gamma, so waiting always loses value
Under the risk-neutral measure the stock drifts down, so waiting is costly

cards.name: Dividends and early exercise
cards.prompt: For an American call on a dividend-paying stock, when can early exercise be optimal?
cards.answer: Only just before an ex-dividend date
cards.explanation:
Between dividend dates the stock behaves like a non-dividend stock, and the same argument shows waiting is better.
The only thing exercising can gain is the upcoming dividend, which the option holder otherwise misses when the price drops on the ex-date. So the only candidate exercise times are the moments just before ex-dividend dates.
distractors: At any time once the call is deep in the money
Only right after an ex-dividend date
Never; dividends do not change the argument

cards.name: Put price arbitrage (B)
cards.prompt: A non-dividend stock has two European puts with the same expiry: strike 80 priced at USD 8, and strike 90 priced at USD 9. Is there an arbitrage? If so, how do you trade it?
cards.answer: Yes: sell 9 puts at $K=80$ and buy 8 puts at $K=90$ (zero cost, payoff $\ge0$)
cards.explanation:
A put's price is convex in the strike, and a zero-strike put is worthless, so $P(\lambda K)\le\lambda P(K)$ for $0<\lambda<1$.
With $\lambda=8/9$, $P(80)$ should be at most $\tfrac89\cdot9=8$, and strictly less, since the 90-strike put is worth extra when $S_T$ lands between 80 and 90. At 8, the 80-strike put is too expensive.
Selling 9 of them and buying 8 of the 90-strike puts costs $72-72=0$. Payoff at expiry:
- $S_T\ge90$: 0.
- $80\le S_T<90$: $8(90-S_T)\ge0$.
- $S_T<80$: $8(90-S_T)-9(80-S_T)=S_T>0$.
The payoff is never negative and sometimes positive, so this is an arbitrage.
distractors: No: the prices are consistent, since both cost 10% of the strike
Yes: buy 9 puts at $K=80$ and sell 8 puts at $K=90$ (zero cost, payoff $\ge0$)
Yes: buy 1 put at $K=80$, sell 1 put at $K=90$ and pocket the USD 1 credit
cards.hint: Put prices are convex in the strike and a zero-strike put is worthless.

cards.name: Black-Scholes-Merton PDE
cards.prompt: Write the Black-Scholes-Merton PDE satisfied by the price $V(S,t)$ of a derivative on a non-dividend stock (subscripts denote partial derivatives).
cards.answer: $V_t+rSV_S+\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}=rV$
cards.explanation:
The stock's real-world drift $\mu$ does not appear: hedging removes it, and the risk-free rate $r$ takes its place.
In Greek notation the PDE reads $\Theta+rS\Delta+\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma=rV$. It holds for any derivative whose value depends only on $S$ and $t$; the specific payoff enters only through the terminal condition.
distractors: $V_t+\mu SV_S+\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}=rV$
$V_t+rSV_S+\tfrac12\sigma^2SV_{SS}=rV$
$V_t+rSV_S-\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}=rV$

cards.name: Deriving the BSM PDE
cards.prompt: Briefly explain how to derive the Black-Scholes-Merton PDE, assuming $dS=\mu S\,dt+\sigma S\,dW$.
cards.answer: Hold one derivative, short $\partial V/\partial S$ shares: $dW$ cancels, so the portfolio earns $r$
cards.explanation:
By Ito's lemma, $dV=(V_t+\mu SV_S+\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS})\,dt+\sigma SV_S\,dW$.
Form $\Pi=V-V_SS$. Then $d\Pi=dV-V_S\,dS=(V_t+\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS})\,dt$: both the random term and the $\mu$ term cancel.
A riskless portfolio must earn the risk-free rate, so $d\Pi=r(V-V_SS)\,dt$.
Setting the two equal gives $V_t+rSV_S+\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}=rV$.
distractors: Hold one derivative, long $\partial V/\partial S$ shares: $dW$ cancels, so the portfolio earns $\mu$
Take real-world expectations in Ito's formula and set the drift of $V$ to $\mu V$
Hold one derivative, short $\partial^2V/\partial S^2$ shares: $dt$ cancels, so it earns $r$

cards.name: Feynman-Kac theorem
cards.prompt: Let $dX=\beta(t,X)\,dt+\gamma(t,X)\,dW$ and $V(t,x)=E[e^{-r(T-t)}f(X_T)\mid X_t=x]$. By the discounted Feynman-Kac theorem, what PDE does $V$ satisfy?
cards.answer: $V_t+\beta V_x+\tfrac12\gamma^2V_{xx}=rV$ with $V(T,x)=f(x)$
cards.explanation:
Feynman-Kac connects conditional expectations of diffusions to PDEs.
Under the risk-neutral measure the stock follows $dS=rS\,dt+\sigma S\,dW$. Plugging in $\beta=rS$ and $\gamma=\sigma S$ gives exactly the Black-Scholes-Merton PDE. So pricing by risk-neutral expectation and pricing by solving the PDE give the same answer.
distractors: $V_t+\beta V_x+\tfrac12\gamma V_{xx}=rV$ with $V(T,x)=f(x)$
$V_t+\beta V_x+\tfrac12\gamma^2V_{xx}=0$ with $V(0,x)=f(x)$
$V_t-\beta V_x+\tfrac12\gamma^2V_{xx}=rV$ with $V(T,x)=f(x)$

cards.name: Black-Scholes formula
cards.prompt: Give the Black-Scholes prices of a European call and a European put on a stock with continuous dividend yield $y$.
cards.answer: $c=Se^{-y\tau}N(d_1)-Ke^{-r\tau}N(d_2)$, $p=Ke^{-r\tau}N(-d_2)-Se^{-y\tau}N(-d_1)$
cards.explanation:
Here $\tau=T-t$ and $N$ is the standard normal CDF.
The call is long $N(d_1)$ units of the dividend-discounted stock and short $N(d_2)$ units of the discounted strike.
The put follows from put-call parity $c-p=Se^{-y\tau}-Ke^{-r\tau}$ and the identity $1-N(x)=N(-x)$. Setting $y=0$ gives the original formulas.
distractors: $c=Se^{-y\tau}N(d_2)-Ke^{-r\tau}N(d_1)$, $p=Ke^{-r\tau}N(-d_1)-Se^{-y\tau}N(-d_2)$
$c=Se^{-r\tau}N(d_1)-Ke^{-y\tau}N(d_2)$, $p=Ke^{-y\tau}N(-d_2)-Se^{-r\tau}N(-d_1)$
$c=Se^{-y\tau}N(d_1)-Ke^{-r\tau}N(d_2)$, $p=Se^{-y\tau}N(-d_1)-Ke^{-r\tau}N(-d_2)$

cards.name: Black-Scholes d1 and d2
cards.prompt: In the Black-Scholes formula with dividend yield $y$, what are $d_1$ and $d_2$?
cards.answer: $d_{1,2}=\frac{\ln(S/K)+(r-y\pm\sigma^2/2)\tau}{\sigma\sqrt\tau}$, so $d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt\tau$
cards.explanation:
Equivalently, $d_1=\frac{\ln(Se^{-y\tau}/K)+(r+\sigma^2/2)\tau}{\sigma\sqrt\tau}$. The plus sign goes with $d_1$ and the minus sign with $d_2$.
$N(d_2)$ is the risk-neutral probability that $S_T>K$, and $e^{-y\tau}N(d_1)$ is the call's delta.
distractors: $d_{1,2}=\frac{\ln(K/S)+(r-y\pm\sigma^2/2)\tau}{\sigma\sqrt\tau}$, so $d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt\tau$
$d_{1,2}=\frac{\ln(S/K)+(r+y\pm\sigma^2/2)\tau}{\sigma\sqrt\tau}$, so $d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt\tau$
$d_{1,2}=\frac{\ln(S/K)+(r-y\pm\sigma^2/2)\tau}{\sigma^2\tau}$, so $d_2=d_1-\sigma^2\tau$

cards.name: BS yield for futures and FX
cards.prompt: When you apply the dividend-yield Black-Scholes formula to options on a futures contract and to options on a foreign currency, what yield $y$ do you use?
cards.answer: Futures: $y=r$; foreign currency: $y=r_f$ (foreign risk-free rate)
cards.explanation:
A futures contract costs nothing to enter, so under the risk-neutral measure its price has zero drift. That is the same as an asset whose yield equals $r$ (Black's model).
Holding foreign currency earns the foreign interest rate $r_f$, which acts like a continuous dividend yield (Garman-Kohlhagen).
distractors: Futures: $y=0$; foreign currency: $y=r_f$ (foreign risk-free rate)
Futures: $y=r$; foreign currency: $y=r-r_f$
Futures: $y=r_f$; foreign currency: $y=r$

cards.name: Black-Scholes assumptions (A)
cards.prompt: What assumptions underlie the original Black-Scholes formula for European options?
cards.answer: GBM stock with constant $\mu,\sigma$; constant known $r$; no dividends, costs, taxes or arbitrage
cards.explanation:
The standard list:
- The stock follows geometric Brownian motion $dS=\mu S\,dt+\sigma S\,dW$ with constant $\mu$ and $\sigma$, so $S_T$ is lognormal.
- The risk-free rate is constant and known.
- The stock pays no dividends during the option's life.
- There are no transaction costs or taxes, and short-sale proceeds can be fully invested.
- Securities are perfectly divisible and can be traded continuously.
- There are no riskless arbitrage opportunities.
distractors: Normally distributed stock price; constant $r$; no dividends; American exercise allowed
GBM stock with stochastic $\sigma$; constant $r$; dividends paid continuously
GBM stock with constant $\mu,\sigma$; stochastic $r$; proportional transaction costs

cards.name: BS via risk-neutral pricing (B)
cards.prompt: How do you derive the Black-Scholes price of a European call on a non-dividend stock using the risk-neutral measure?
cards.answer: Write $S_T=Se^{(r-\sigma^2/2)\tau+\sigma\sqrt\tau\,\varepsilon}$ and compute $e^{-r\tau}\tilde E[(S_T-K)^+]$
cards.explanation:
Under the risk-neutral measure $dS=rS\,dt+\sigma S\,dW$, so $\ln S_T\sim N(\ln S+(r-\sigma^2/2)\tau,\ \sigma^2\tau)$ and $\varepsilon\sim N(0,1)$.
The call finishes in the money exactly when $\varepsilon>-d_2$, so
$$\tilde E[(S_T-K)^+]=\int_{-d_2}^{\infty}\big(Se^{(r-\sigma^2/2)\tau+\sigma\sqrt\tau\varepsilon}-K\big)\phi(\varepsilon)\,d\varepsilon.$$
The $K$ term gives $KN(d_2)$. In the $S$ term, complete the square (shift $\varepsilon$ by $\sigma\sqrt\tau$) to get $Se^{r\tau}N(d_1)$.
Discounting gives $c=SN(d_1)-Ke^{-r\tau}N(d_2)$.
distractors: Write $S_T=Se^{(\mu-\sigma^2/2)\tau+\sigma\sqrt\tau\,\varepsilon}$ and compute $e^{-\mu\tau}E[(S_T-K)^+]$
Write $S_T=Se^{r\tau+\sigma\sqrt\tau\,\varepsilon}$ and compute $e^{-r\tau}\tilde E[(S_T-K)^+]$
Write $S_T=S+r\tau+\sigma\sqrt\tau\,\varepsilon$ and compute $e^{-r\tau}\tilde E[(S_T-K)^+]$

cards.name: Meaning of N(d2)
cards.prompt: In the Black-Scholes call formula $c=SN(d_1)-Ke^{-r\tau}N(d_2)$, what is the probabilistic meaning of $N(d_2)$?
cards.answer: The risk-neutral probability that the call finishes in the money ($S_T>K$)
cards.explanation:
In the risk-neutral derivation the strike term is $K\,\tilde P(\varepsilon>-d_2)=K(1-N(-d_2))=KN(d_2)$, and $\{\varepsilon>-d_2\}$ is exactly the event $S_T>K$.
By contrast, $N(d_1)$ is the delta (and the in-the-money probability under the measure that uses the stock as numeraire).
Because it uses the risk-neutral drift $r$ rather than $\mu$, $N(d_2)$ is not the real-world probability.
distractors: The real-world probability that the call finishes in the money ($S_T>K$)
The risk-neutral probability that the put finishes in the money ($S_T<K$)
The call's delta, i.e. the shares held in the replicating portfolio

cards.name: BS via the heat equation (C)
cards.prompt: Which change of variables turns the Black-Scholes-Merton PDE (non-dividend stock) into the heat equation, and what is the resulting equation?
cards.answer: $\tau=T-t$, $u=e^{r\tau}V$, $x=\ln S+(r-\tfrac12\sigma^2)\tau$ give $u_\tau=\tfrac12\sigma^2u_{xx}$
cards.explanation:
Each substitution removes one feature:
- $y=\ln S$ turns the coefficients $S$ and $S^2$ into constants (geometric becomes arithmetic Brownian motion).
- $\tau=T-t$ turns the terminal payoff into an initial condition.
- $u=e^{r\tau}V$ removes the $-rV$ term.
- $x=y+(r-\tfrac12\sigma^2)\tau$ removes the first-derivative (drift) term.
The heat equation is solved by convolving the initial condition $\max(e^{x}-K,0)$ with a Gaussian kernel of variance $\sigma^2\tau$. The integral is the same one as in the risk-neutral derivation, giving $c=SN(d_1)-Ke^{-r\tau}N(d_2)$.
distractors: $\tau=T-t$, $u=e^{-r\tau}V$, $x=\ln S-(r-\tfrac12\sigma^2)\tau$ give $u_\tau=\tfrac12\sigma^2u_{xx}$
$\tau=T-t$, $u=e^{r\tau}V$, $x=S+(r-\tfrac12\sigma^2)\tau$ give $u_\tau=\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2u_{xx}$
$\tau=T-t$, $u=e^{r\tau}V$, $x=\ln S+(r-\tfrac12\sigma^2)\tau$ give $u_\tau=-\tfrac12\sigma^2u_{xx}$

cards.name: Pay 1 at first hit of H (D)
cards.prompt: Interest rates are zero, and a non-dividend stock trades at USD 20. An option pays USD 1 the first time the stock price reaches USD 50. What is the option worth today, in dollars?
cards.explanation:
With $r=0$, the stock is a martingale under the risk-neutral measure. Stop it the first time it reaches 50 (it may instead drift toward 0 and never get there). Optional stopping gives $p\cdot50+(1-p)\cdot0=20$, so the probability of ever hitting 50 is $p=20/50=0.4$. With zero rates, the option is worth USD 0.40. In general the value is $S_0/H$.
No-arbitrage check: $1/50$ of a share costs 0.40 and is worth exactly 1 when the stock reaches 50, so the option can't cost more than that. If it cost $C<0.4$, you could buy it by shorting $C/20$ shares: zero cost now, and $1-50C/20>0$ when the level is hit.
Side note: $\tilde E[S_T]=20$ for every $T$, yet $\ln S$ drifts down at rate $\sigma^2/2$, so $\tilde P(S_T\ge20)\to0$ as $T\to\infty$.

cards.name: Contract paying 1/S_T (E)
cards.prompt: A non-dividend stock follows GBM with volatility $\sigma$, and the risk-free rate is $r$. What is the value at time $t$ of a contract that pays $1/S_T$ at maturity $T$ ($\tau=T-t$)?
cards.answer: $\frac{1}{S_t}e^{(\sigma^2-2r)\tau}$
cards.explanation:
Under the risk-neutral measure $\ln S_T=\ln S_t+(r-\tfrac12\sigma^2)\tau+\sigma\sqrt\tau Z$. So $\ln(1/S_T)$ is normal with mean $-\ln S_t-(r-\tfrac12\sigma^2)\tau$ and variance $\sigma^2\tau$, which gives
$$\tilde E[1/S_T]=\frac{1}{S_t}e^{-(r-\sigma^2/2)\tau+\sigma^2\tau/2}=\frac{1}{S_t}e^{(\sigma^2-r)\tau}.$$
Discounting by $e^{-r\tau}$ gives $\frac{1}{S_t}e^{(\sigma^2-2r)\tau}$. Ito's lemma on $V=1/S$ confirms it: $dV=(\sigma^2-r)V\,dt-\sigma V\,dW$.
The answer exceeds the naive guess $e^{-r\tau}/F=\frac{1}{S_t}e^{-2r\tau}$ (with $F=S_te^{r\tau}$) because $1/x$ is convex.

cards.name: Delta formulas
cards.prompt: What are the deltas of a European call and a European put on a stock with continuous dividend yield $y$?

cards.explanation:
Call delta lies between 0 and $e^{-y\tau}$, and put delta between $-e^{-y\tau}$ and 0.

cards.name: Delta of a call (A)
cards.prompt: What is the delta of a European call on a non-dividend stock, and what is the subtle step in deriving it from $c=SN(d_1)-Ke^{-r\tau}N(d_2)$?
cards.answer: $\Delta=N(d_1)$; the terms from $\partial d_{1,2}/\partial S$ cancel since $SN'(d_1)=Ke^{-r\tau}N'(d_2)$
cards.explanation:
The common mistake is to treat $N(d_1)$ and $N(d_2)$ as constants. Done properly,
$$\frac{\partial c}{\partial S}=N(d_1)+SN'(d_1)\frac{\partial d_1}{\partial S}-Ke^{-r\tau}N'(d_2)\frac{\partial d_2}{\partial S}.$$
Both $d_1$ and $d_2$ have derivative $\frac{1}{S\sigma\sqrt\tau}$ with respect to $S$. Using $d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt\tau$ and expanding the exponent, $N'(d_2)=N'(d_1)\frac{S}{K}e^{r\tau}$. So $SN'(d_1)=Ke^{-r\tau}N'(d_2)$, the last two terms cancel, and $\Delta=N(d_1)$.

$\Delta=N(d_1)+SN'(d_1)$; only $d_1$ depends on $S$, so its extra term survives

cards.name: Delta of an ATM call (B)
cards.prompt: What value does the delta of an at-the-money ($S=K$) European call on a non-dividend stock approach as expiry nears ($\tau\to0$)?
cards.answer: 0.5 (before expiry it sits slightly above 0.5, since $d_1>0$ when $r>0$)
cards.explanation:
With $S=K$, $d_1=\left(\frac{r}{\sigma}+\frac{\sigma}{2}\right)\sqrt\tau>0$, so $\Delta=N(d_1)>0.5$, and longer maturities push it higher. As $\tau\to0$, $d_1\to0$ and $\Delta\to N(0)=0.5$. With a dividend yield $y<r$, $d_1$ is still positive.
More generally, $\Delta\to1$ for $S\gg K$ and $\Delta\to0$ for $S\ll K$. The shorter the maturity, the faster delta reaches these limits, so the delta curve steepens around $K$.

cards.name: Dynamic delta hedging (C)
cards.prompt: You buy a European call on GM stock and want to delta-hedge it dynamically. How do you set up the hedge, and how do you rebalance after a sudden rise in GM's price?
cards.answer: Short $\Delta=e^{-y\tau}N(d_1)$ shares per call and lend the extra cash; after a rise, short more
cards.explanation:
Delta increases with $S$ (because $d_1$ does). After GM jumps, the call's delta is larger, so you must short additional shares to stay delta-neutral.
Shorting $\Delta$ shares brings in more cash than the call costs. Under Black-Scholes the surplus is $Se^{-y\tau}N(d_1)-c=Ke^{-r\tau}N(d_2)$, which you lend at $r$; this amount also grows after the rise.
A delta hedge matches only the option's value and slope. To hedge its curvature you also need to hedge gamma.

cards.name: Value of an ATM call (D)
cards.prompt: A non-dividend stock trades at USD 100 with volatility $\sigma=20\%$, and interest rates are close to zero. Using the short-maturity approximation for an at-the-money call (with $1/\sqrt{2\pi}\approx0.4$), estimate the price of a 3-month at-the-money European call.
cards.answer: USD 4, from $c\approx0.4\,\sigma S\sqrt\tau$

With $S=K$ and $r\approx0$, $c\approx S[N(d_1)-N(d_2)]$ with $d_{1,2}=\left(\frac{r}{\sigma}\pm\frac{\sigma}{2}\right)\sqrt\tau$, both near 0. The normal density there is about $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$, so
$$N(d_1)-N(d_2)\approx\frac{d_1-d_2}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac{\sigma\sqrt\tau}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\approx0.4\,\sigma\sqrt\tau.$$
Here $c\approx0.4\times0.2\times100\times\sqrt{0.25}=4$ dollars. The exact Black-Scholes price with $r=0$ is about 3.99, so the rule of thumb is very close. Traders also use it in reverse to read implied volatility off at-the-money prices.

cards.name: Gamma formula
cards.prompt: What is the gamma of a European call or put on a stock with dividend yield $y$, and what is its sign?
cards.answer: $\Gamma=\frac{e^{-y\tau}N'(d_1)}{S\sigma\sqrt\tau}$, the same for call and put, always positive

cards.name: Gamma of ATM option near expiry

cards.name: Gamma vs. moneyness and maturity
cards.prompt: How does gamma depend on moneyness? How does maturity affect gamma for options near the strike versus far from it?
cards.answer: Peaks near the strike; near $K$ shorter maturity means higher gamma, far from $K$ longer maturity does

cards.prompt: Give the Black-Scholes theta of a European call on a stock with dividend yield $y$.

cards.prompt: For a European call on a non-dividend stock, what is the sign of theta, and how does theta behave deep out of the money, deep in the money and at the money?

cards.name: Positive theta (A)
cards.prompt: When can a European option have positive theta?

American options, and European calls on non-dividend stocks, always have negative theta.

cards.name: Delta-neutral long call (B)
cards.prompt: You are long a call on GM (no dividends) and short enough GM shares to be delta-neutral. If GM's price immediately jumps, either up or down, what happens to the value of your portfolio?
cards.answer: It increases either way (long gamma); not an arbitrage, since negative theta pays for it
cards.explanation:
Shares have zero gamma, so the hedged position keeps the option's positive gamma. Its value is convex in $S$, so any immediate move, up or down, produces a gain.
But the BSM PDE implies that a delta-neutral portfolio satisfies $\Theta+\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma=r\Pi$. cards.name: Theta-gamma relation
cards.prompt: For a delta-neutral portfolio of value $\Pi$, what relationship between theta and gamma does the Black-Scholes-Merton PDE imply?
cards.answer: $\Theta+\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma=r\Pi$

In Greek form the PDE reads $\Theta+rS\Delta+\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma=r\Pi$, and $\Delta=0$ removes the middle term.
When $r\Pi$ is small, theta and gamma must have opposite signs: being long gamma means paying time decay, and being short gamma means collecting it. For example, an at-the-money option near expiry has a very large positive gamma and a very negative theta.

cards.prompt: What is the vega of a European call or put on a stock with dividend yield $y$? Which options have the most vega, and how does vega change as expiry nears?

cards.name: Implied volatility and smile (A)
cards.prompt: Explain implied volatility and the volatility smile. What does the smile imply for the Black-Scholes model?
cards.answer: IV is the $\sigma$ that makes BS match the market price; it varies by strike, so BS's constant vol is wrong
cards.explanation:
Implied volatility is found by inverting the Black-Scholes formula at the observed option price.
Plotting implied volatility against strike for one expiry gives a smile or a skew. For currencies, in- and out-of-the-money options have higher implied volatility than at-the-money ones. For equities, implied volatility usually falls as the strike rises.

cards.name: Constant vs. random volatility (B)
cards.prompt: You can price a European call either with a constant volatility of 30% or with a volatility drawn at random from a distribution with mean 30%. Which call is more expensive?
cards.answer: Usually the random-vol one, since $c$ is convex in $\sigma$ when $d_1d_2>0$, but not always
cards.explanation:
By Jensen's inequality, $E[c(\sigma)]\ge c(E[\sigma])$ whenever $c$ is convex in $\sigma$. Vega $\nu=S\sqrt\tau N'(d_1)$ is always positive, and volga is
$$\frac{\partial^2c}{\partial\sigma^2}=\nu\,\frac{d_1d_2}{\sigma}.$$
For most in-the-money calls both $d$'s are positive, and for most out-of-the-money calls both are negative, so $d_1d_2>0$ and randomizing $\sigma$ adds value.
Near the money, however, we can have $d_1>0>d_2$. Then volga is negative and the constant-volatility call can be worth more.

cards.name: Risk-neutral density from calls (C)
cards.prompt: You don't know the process the stock follows, but you observe European call prices $c(K)$ for every strike $K$ with maturity $T$. How do you recover the risk-neutral density of $S_T$?
cards.answer: $f_{S_T}(K)=e^{r\tau}\,\frac{\partial^2c}{\partial K^2}$
cards.explanation:

- $\frac{\partial c}{\partial K}=-e^{-r\tau}\int_K^\infty f(s)\,ds=-e^{-r\tau}\tilde P(S_T>K)$.
- $\frac{\partial^2c}{\partial K^2}=e^{-r\tau}f(K)$.
This is the Breeden-Litzenberger result. It needs no model for the stock, only a continuum of strikes.

cards.name: Bull spread construction
cards.prompt: How is a bull call spread built, and what does it pay at expiry?

cards.name: Binary call price

cards.name: Binary call via call spread
cards.prompt: How can you approximately replicate a digital call paying USD 1 if $S_T>K$ with vanilla calls, and what is the drawback?
cards.answer: Buy $\frac1{2\epsilon}$ calls at $K-\epsilon$, sell as many at $K+\epsilon$; needs many options and fine strikes
cards.explanation:
This tight call spread pays 0 below $K-\epsilon$, rises linearly to 1 between the two strikes, and pays exactly 1 above $K+\epsilon$. It matches the digital everywhere except in that narrow band, and it converges to the digital as $\epsilon\to0$ (the limit is $-\partial c/\partial K$).
In practice, strikes aren't available at arbitrarily fine spacing, and a small $\epsilon$ requires a large number $\frac1{2\epsilon}$ of options.
distractors: Buy $\frac1{2\epsilon}$ calls at $K+\epsilon$, sell as many at $K-\epsilon$; needs many options and fine strikes
Buy $2\epsilon$ calls at $K-\epsilon$, sell as many at $K+\epsilon$; exact for any $\epsilon$
Buy one call and sell one put, both at $K$; exact replication, with no drawback

cards.name: Exchange options
cards.prompt: Price an exchange option paying $\max(S_{1,T}-S_{2,T},0)$, where $S_1$ and $S_2$ are non-dividend stocks following GBMs with volatilities $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ and correlation $\rho$.
cards.answer: $S_1N(d_1)-S_2N(d_2)$ with vol $\sqrt{\sigma_1^2-2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2+\sigma_2^2}$ and $r=0$
cards.explanation:
Use $S_2$ as the numeraire: the payoff is $S_{2,T}\max(S_{1,T}/S_{2,T}-1,0)$.
The ratio $f=S_1/S_2$ is a GBM. Under the measure that uses $S_2$ as numeraire it is a martingale with volatility $\sigma=\sqrt{\sigma_1^2-2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2+\sigma_2^2}$, the volatility of $\ln S_1-\ln S_2$.
So the option, measured in units of $S_2$, is a Black-Scholes call on $f$ with strike 1 and a zero interest rate:
$$\frac{V}{S_2}=fN(d_1)-N(d_2),\quad d_{1,2}=\frac{\ln(S_1/S_2)\pm\tfrac12\sigma^2\tau}{\sigma\sqrt\tau}.$$
Multiplying by $S_2$ gives Margrabe's formula, in which the interest rate drops out. The book's worked solution prices the mirror payoff $\max(S_2-S_1,0)$ with $S_1$ as numeraire; it's the same formula with the roles swapped.
distractors: $S_1N(d_1)-S_2N(d_2)$ with vol $\sqrt{\sigma_1^2+2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2+\sigma_2^2}$ and $r=0$
$S_1N(d_1)-S_2e^{-r\tau}N(d_2)$ with vol $\sqrt{\sigma_1^2-2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2+\sigma_2^2}$
$S_1N(d_1)-S_2N(d_2)$ with vol $\sigma_1-\sigma_2$ and $r=0$
cards.hint: Change numeraire so that only the ratio of the two stocks matters.

cards.name: Minimum-variance portfolio
cards.prompt: Stocks A and B both have an expected return of 12%. A's return has a standard deviation of 20%, B's has 30%, and their correlation is 0.5. What fraction of your investment should go into A to minimize portfolio risk?
cards.explanation:
With equal expected returns, only variance matters. For weight $w$ in A,
$$\sigma_p^2=w^2\sigma_A^2+(1-w)^2\sigma_B^2+2w(1-w)\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B.$$
Setting the derivative to zero gives $w=\frac{\sigma_B^2-\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B}{\sigma_A^2-2\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B+\sigma_B^2}=\frac{0.09-0.03}{0.04-0.06+0.09}=\frac{0.06}{0.07}=\frac67$.
The resulting portfolio volatility is about 19.6%, slightly below A's 20%.

cards.name: Two-asset min-variance weight
cards.prompt: For two assets with volatilities $\sigma_A,\sigma_B$ and correlation $\rho$, what weight in A minimizes the variance of a fully invested portfolio?
cards.answer: $w_A=\frac{\sigma_B^2-\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B}{\sigma_A^2-2\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B+\sigma_B^2}$
cards.explanation:
Minimize $w^2\sigma_A^2+(1-w)^2\sigma_B^2+2w(1-w)\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B$ over $w$.
The numerator uses B's variance: the riskier B is, the more weight goes to A. The weight exceeds 1 (meaning you short B) when $\rho>\sigma_A/\sigma_B$.
distractors: $w_A=\frac{\sigma_A^2-\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B}{\sigma_A^2-2\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B+\sigma_B^2}$
$w_A=\frac{\sigma_B^2+\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B}{\sigma_A^2+2\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B+\sigma_B^2}$
$w_A=\frac{\sigma_B^2-\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B}{\sigma_A^2+\sigma_B^2}$

cards.name: Markowitz mean-variance problem
cards.prompt: State the Markowitz mean-variance problem for portfolio weights $w$ with target expected return $\mu_p$, where $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix, $\mu$ the vector of mean returns and $e$ the all-ones vector.
cards.answer: $\min_w w^T\Sigma w$ s.t. $w^T\mu=\mu_p,\ w^Te=1$
cards.explanation:
The portfolio mean is $w^T\mu$ and the variance is $w^T\Sigma w=\sum_i w_i^2\sigma_i^2+\sum_{i\ne j}w_iw_j\sigma_{ij}$.
Efficient portfolios minimize variance for each target return, and varying $\mu_p$ traces out the efficient frontier. With only these two equality constraints there is a closed form, $w^*=\lambda\Sigma^{-1}e+\gamma\Sigma^{-1}\mu$, where the scalars $\lambda,\gamma$ are set by the constraints.
distractors: $\max_w w^T\mu$ s.t. $w^T\Sigma w=\mu_p,\ w^Te=1$
$\min_w w^T\Sigma w$ s.t. $w^T\mu=\mu_p$ only (no budget constraint)
$\min_w w^T\mu$ s.t. $w^T\Sigma w=\mu_p,\ w^Te=1$

cards.name: Value at risk
cards.prompt: Briefly explain Value at Risk (VaR) at confidence level $\alpha$ (for example 95% or 99%).
cards.answer: The loss over the horizon that is exceeded only with probability $1-\alpha$
cards.explanation:
VaR is a quantile: $P(\text{loss}>\text{VaR})=1-\alpha$. Equivalently, it is the negative of the $(1-\alpha)$ percentile of the P&L distribution, i.e. the 5th percentile at 95% or the 1st percentile at 99%.
Its appeal is that it sums up risk as a single dollar figure for a given horizon and confidence level.
The expected loss beyond that quantile is a different measure: expected shortfall, or CVaR.
distractors: The expected loss over the horizon, given that losses exceed the $\alpha$ quantile
The largest possible loss over the horizon
The standard deviation of P&L over the horizon, scaled by $\alpha$

cards.name: VaR drawback: tail blindness
cards.prompt: You are short protection on a USD 1M credit default swap on bond A, which has a 3% default probability over the horizon and zero recovery. What is the 95% VaR of this position, in dollars?
cards.answer: USD 0: the 3% default chance is below 5%, so VaR misses the USD 1M tail loss
cards.explanation:
With probability 97% there is no loss, so the 5th percentile of P&L is 0 and the 95% VaR is 0, even though there is a 3% chance of losing the entire USD 1M.
Because VaR looks at only one quantile, it says nothing about how bad losses are beyond it. For derivatives with highly non-normal, fat-tailed or jumpy P&L, this can badly understate risk, which is why stress tests are used alongside VaR.
distractors: USD 1,000,000, since any default loses the full notional
USD 30,000, the expected loss
USD 50,000, i.e. 5% of the notional

cards.name: VaR is not subadditive
cards.prompt: Add a second short USD 1M CDS position on bond B (3% default probability, zero recovery, independent of A). Each position alone has a 95% VaR of 0. What is the 95% VaR of the combined portfolio, in millions of dollars?
cards.answer: USD 1M, since P(at least one default) $=1-0.97^2\approx5.91\%>5\%$
cards.explanation:
$P(\text{at least one default})=1-0.97^2=5.91\%$, which exceeds 5%. So the 5th percentile of P&L is a loss of USD 1M (both defaulting has only a 0.09% chance).
So $\text{VaR}(A+B)>\text{VaR}(A)+\text{VaR}(B)$: combining the positions appears to increase risk, which contradicts the idea that diversification shouldn't. This failure of subadditivity means VaR is not a coherent risk measure.
distractors: 0, since each position alone has zero VaR and VaRs add
USD 2M, since both bonds could default together
USD 0.06M, the sum of the two expected losses

cards.name: Coherent risk measures
cards.prompt: Which four properties define a coherent risk measure $\rho$, and which common measure satisfies them all where VaR does not?
cards.answer: Subadditive, positively homogeneous, monotone, translation invariant; CVaR (expected shortfall)
cards.explanation:
The axioms of Artzner et al., for positions $X,Y$:
- Subadditivity: $\rho(X+Y)\le\rho(X)+\rho(Y)$.
- Positive homogeneity: $\rho(aX)=a\rho(X)$ for $a>0$.
- Monotonicity: if $X\le Y$ in every state, then $\rho(X)\ge\rho(Y)$.
- Translation invariance: $\rho(X+k)=\rho(X)-k$ for a cash amount $k$.
VaR can violate subadditivity, while conditional VaR satisfies all four.
distractors: Subadditive, positively homogeneous, monotone, translation invariant; 99% VaR
Additive, convex, symmetric, translation invariant; standard deviation
Superadditive, homogeneous, monotone, translation invariant; CVaR (expected shortfall)

cards.name: Duration and convexity
cards.prompt: Define a bond's duration and convexity in terms of its price $P(y)$ and yield $y$ (primes denote derivatives with respect to $y$), and give the second-order approximation for the price change.
cards.answer: $D=-P'/P$, $C=P''/P$, $\Delta P/P\approx-D\,\Delta y+\tfrac12C\,\Delta y^2$
cards.explanation:
Duration is the percentage price sensitivity to yield, with a sign flip; convexity is the curvature. The formula is a second-order Taylor expansion of $P(y)$, and for small $\Delta y$, $\Delta P/P\approx-D\Delta y$.
Positive convexity means the price rises more when yields fall than it drops when yields rise by the same amount.
distractors: $D=P'/P$, $C=P''/P$, $\Delta P/P\approx D\,\Delta y+\tfrac12C\,\Delta y^2$
$D=-P'/P$, $C=P''/P$, $\Delta P/P\approx-D\,\Delta y-\tfrac12C\,\Delta y^2$
$D=-P'$, $C=P''$, $\Delta P/P\approx-D\,\Delta y+C\,\Delta y^2$

cards.name: What drives duration and convexity
cards.prompt: For a fixed-rate coupon bond, how do duration and convexity typically change when (a) maturity $T$ increases, (b) the coupon rate $c$ increases, (c) the yield $y$ increases?
cards.answer: Longer $T$: both up; higher coupon: both down; higher yield: both down
cards.explanation:
Duration is a present-value-weighted average time of the cash flows.
- Longer maturity pushes cash flows later.
- A higher coupon puts more weight on early cash flows, shortening it.
- A higher yield discounts distant cash flows more heavily, also shortening it.
Convexity moves in the same directions. One exception: for some deep-discount long bonds, duration can dip slightly as maturity grows.
distractors: Longer $T$: both up; higher coupon: both up; higher yield: both down
Longer $T$: both down; higher coupon: both down; higher yield: both up
Longer $T$: both up; higher coupon: both down; higher yield: both up

cards.name: Dollar duration and DV01
cards.prompt: Define dollar duration and DV01. Why is dollar duration preferred for instruments such as swaps?
cards.answer: Dollar duration $=-dP/dy=PD$; DV01 $=-\frac{dP}{dy}/10{,}000$; a swap can have $P=0$, so $D$ fails
cards.explanation:
DV01 is the price change for a one-basis-point (0.0001) move in yield.
Duration divides by price, so it breaks down for positions worth about zero, such as an at-market swap, while dollar duration still measures the rate exposure. Dollar durations are also additive across positions.
distractors: Dollar duration $=D/P$; DV01 $=-\frac{dP}{dy}/100$; a swap's duration is constant
Dollar duration $=-dP/dy=PD$; DV01 $=-\frac{dP}{dy}\times10{,}000$; swaps have no rate risk
Dollar duration $=PD^2$; DV01 $=-\frac{dP}{dy}/10{,}000$; a swap always trades at par

cards.name: Portfolio duration
cards.prompt: A portfolio holds bonds with values $P_i$ (total $P$), durations $D_i$ and convexities $C_i$. What are the portfolio's duration, convexity and dollar duration?
cards.answer: $D=\sum\frac{P_i}{P}D_i$, $C=\sum\frac{P_i}{P}C_i$; dollar duration is the sum of the dollar durations
cards.explanation:
The portfolio price is $P=\sum P_i$, so $dP/dy=\sum dP_i/dy$: dollar durations simply add.
Dividing by $P$ turns that sum into a value-weighted average of the individual durations. The same logic applies to convexity.
distractors: $D=\sum D_i$, $C=\sum C_i$; dollar duration is the value-weighted average of dollar durations
$D=\frac1n\sum D_i$, $C=\frac1n\sum C_i$; dollar duration is the sum of the dollar durations
$D=\sum\frac{P_i}{P}D_i$, $C=\sum\frac{P_i}{P}C_i^2$; dollar duration is the largest dollar duration

cards.name: Inverse floater price
cards.prompt: An inverse floater has face value USD 100, matures in 5 years, and pays an annual coupon rate of $30\%-3r$ semiannually, where $r$ is the floating rate reset each period. The yield curve is flat at 7.5%. What is its price, in dollars?
cards.answer: USD 100: long 4 par 7.5% fixed-rate bonds, short 3 par floating-rate bonds
cards.explanation:
Each half-year the inverse floater pays $100\cdot\frac{0.30-3r}{2}=15-150r$, and it returns 100 at maturity.
- 4 fixed-rate bonds with a 7.5% coupon pay $4\times3.75=15$ per period and 400 at maturity.
- Shorting 3 floaters costs $3\times50r=150r$ per period and 300 at maturity.
The net is $15-150r$ per period and 100 at the end, an exact match. With a flat 7.5% curve both kinds of bond trade at par, so the price is $4\cdot100-3\cdot100=100$. (This ignores the zero floor on the coupon, which would bind if $r>10\%$.)
distractors: USD 70: long 1 par 7.5% fixed-rate bond, short 3 zero-coupon bonds
USD 130: long 4 par 7.5% fixed-rate bonds, short 3 par floating-rate bonds
USD 400: long 4 par 7.5% fixed-rate bonds; the floating leg is worth nothing
cards.hint: Replicate the cash flows with fixed-rate and floating-rate bonds.

cards.name: Inverse floater duration
cards.prompt: For the same inverse floater (face 100, 5 years, coupon $30\%-3r$ paid semiannually, flat 7.5% curve, price 100), estimate its modified duration.
cards.answer: About 15 (≈ 14.98), far above its 5-year maturity
cards.explanation:
Dollar durations add across the replicating portfolio: $\mathrm{DD}_{inv}=4\,\mathrm{DD}_{fixed}-3\,\mathrm{DD}_{float}$.
- A par floater just after a reset behaves like a 6-month zero paying 103.75, so $\mathrm{DD}_{float}=\frac{0.5\cdot103.75}{1.0375^2}=\frac{50}{1.0375}\approx48.19$.
- A 5-year 7.5% par bond with semiannual coupons has $\mathrm{DD}_{fixed}=-dP/dy\approx410.64$ (modified duration about 4.11).
So $\mathrm{DD}_{inv}\approx1642.6-144.6\approx1498$ and $D_{inv}=1498/100\approx14.98$. Leverage makes an inverse floater far more rate-sensitive than its maturity suggests.
distractors: About 4.1, the same as a 5-year par bond
About 16.4, i.e. 4 times a par bond's duration
About 5, equal to its time to maturity

cards.name: Futures vs. forwards
cards.prompt: What are the main differences between futures and forward contracts?
cards.answer: Futures: exchange-traded, standardized, marked to market daily; forwards: OTC, customizable, settled at end
cards.explanation:
Daily marking to market means futures gains and losses are paid in cash along the way through margin accounts, which reduces counterparty risk.
Forwards are bilateral and flexible in size and date, but they carry counterparty credit risk until settlement.
With deterministic interest rates the two have the same theoretical price; they diverge when rates are random.
distractors: Futures: OTC, customizable, settled at end; forwards: exchange-traded, standardized, marked to market daily
Futures: exchange-traded, settled at end; forwards: OTC, marked to market daily
No structural difference; futures simply have longer maturities than forwards

cards.name: Futures vs. forwards with random rates
cards.prompt: Interest rates are stochastic, and the underlying asset's price is strongly positively correlated with them. Which is higher, the futures price or the forward price?
cards.answer: Futures: daily gains arrive when rates are high and losses when rates are low
cards.explanation:
With positive correlation, a long futures holder receives variation margin when the asset rises, which tends to happen when rates are high, so the cash can be reinvested at a high rate. Losses tend to come when rates are low, so they are cheap to finance.
This systematic advantage makes a long futures position worth more than a long forward, so the futures price must be higher to offset it. With negative correlation the ordering flips, and with deterministic rates the two prices coincide.
distractors: Forwards: daily gains arrive when rates are low and losses when rates are high
They are equal: both equal $Se^{(r+u-y)\tau}$ regardless of rates
Forwards: settling only at maturity avoids reinvestment risk, so they are worth more

cards.name: Forward price with carry
cards.prompt: With deterministic interest rates, what is the forward (= futures) price of an asset with storage cost rate $u$ and yield $y$ (a dividend yield, convenience yield or foreign interest rate)?
cards.answer: $F=Se^{(r+u-y)\tau}$
cards.explanation:
Cost of carry: buying the asset now and holding it to $T$ costs financing at $r$ plus storage at $u$, and earns the yield $y$. No-arbitrage forces the forward price to equal the spot price carried forward at that net rate.
For a foreign currency, $y$ is the foreign risk-free rate $r_f$; for a commodity, $y$ is the convenience yield.
distractors: $F=Se^{(r-u+y)\tau}$
$F=Se^{(r+u+y)\tau}$
$F=Se^{-(r+u-y)\tau}$

cards.name: Classes of interest rate models
cards.prompt: What are two common ways of classifying interest rate models?
cards.answer: Short-rate vs. forward-rate (e.g. HJM) models; equilibrium vs. no-arbitrage models
cards.explanation:
Short-rate models (Vasicek, CIR, Ho-Lee, Hull-White) specify the dynamics of the instantaneous rate $R(t)$. Forward-rate models such as Heath-Jarrow-Morton model the whole forward curve.
No-arbitrage models (Ho-Lee, Hull-White) are calibrated to fit today's term structure exactly. Equilibrium models (Vasicek, CIR) derive the curve from a few parameters and need not match current bond prices.
distractors: Discrete vs. continuous models; real-world vs. risk-neutral models
Short-rate vs. forward-rate (e.g. HJM) models; normal vs. lognormal equity models
Equilibrium vs. no-arbitrage models; European vs. American rate models

cards.name: Vasicek model
cards.prompt: Write the Vasicek short-rate model. What are its key strength and weakness?
cards.answer: $dR=a(b-R)\,dt+\sigma\,dW$: mean-reverting to $b$, but rates can go negative
cards.explanation:
The drift $a(b-R)$ is negative when $R>b$ and positive when $R<b$, pulling the rate toward the long-run level $b$ at speed $a$.
Because the volatility is constant, $R$ is Gaussian and has a positive probability of turning negative. It is an equilibrium model and does not automatically fit the current term structure.
distractors: $dR=a(b-R)\,dt+\sigma\sqrt R\,dW$: mean-reverting to $b$, and rates stay nonnegative
$dR=\theta(t)\,dt+\sigma\,dW$: fits today's curve, but has no mean reversion
$dR=aR\,dt+\sigma R\,dW$: rates stay positive, but there is no mean reversion

cards.name: Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model
cards.prompt: Write the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) short-rate model. How does it improve on Vasicek?
cards.answer: $dR=a(b-R)\,dt+\sigma\sqrt{R}\,dW$: keeps mean reversion but keeps rates nonnegative
cards.explanation:
The diffusion term $\sigma\sqrt R$ shrinks as the rate approaches zero, so the pull toward $b$ dominates and the rate cannot go negative. It stays strictly positive if $2ab\ge\sigma^2$ (the Feller condition).
Like Vasicek, CIR is an equilibrium model and need not fit today's curve.
distractors: $dR=a(b-R)\,dt+\sigma R\,dW$: keeps mean reversion but keeps rates nonnegative
$dR=a(b(t)-R)\,dt+\sigma\,dW$: keeps mean reversion and fits today's curve
$dR=a(b-R)\,dt+\sigma\sqrt{R}\,dW$: drops mean reversion to keep rates positive

cards.name: Ho-Lee model
cards.prompt: Write the Ho-Lee short-rate model and explain the role of its drift.
cards.answer: $dr=\theta(t)\,dt+\sigma\,dW$; $\theta(t)$ is chosen so the model fits today's rate curve
cards.explanation:
Ho-Lee is the simplest no-arbitrage short-rate model: a normal model whose time-dependent drift is calibrated to match current bond prices.
It has no mean reversion, and like Vasicek it allows negative rates.
distractors: $dr=\theta\,dt+\sigma\,dW$ with constant $\theta$; $\theta$ is the long-run mean rate
$dr=a(\theta(t)-r)\,dt+\sigma\,dW$; $\theta(t)$ sets the speed of mean reversion
$dr=\theta(t)\,dt+\sigma\sqrt r\,dW$; $\theta(t)$ keeps rates positive

cards.name: Hull-White model
cards.prompt: Write the Hull-White short-rate model and explain how it differs from Vasicek.
cards.answer: $dR=a(b(t)-R)\,dt+\sigma\,dW$: Vasicek with a time-dependent $b(t)$ fitted to today's curve
cards.explanation:
Hull-White keeps Vasicek's mean reversion and Gaussian dynamics, but the reversion level varies over time so the model is arbitrage-free with respect to the current term structure.
It can be viewed as Ho-Lee with mean reversion added.
distractors: $dR=a(b-R)\,dt+\sigma\sqrt R\,dW$: Vasicek with square-root volatility
$dR=\theta(t)\,dt+\sigma\,dW$: Vasicek without mean reversion
$dR=a(t)(b-R)\,dt+\sigma\,dW$: Vasicek with a time-dependent speed fitted to volatility
